title: Carrie Coon Is Ready for the Crone Years: ‘We’re Going to Dance Naked in the Moonlight’
text: Carrie Coon on 'The Liberation,' 'The Gilded Age,' and Hollywood's Double Standards Subscribe Fashion Beauty Culture Horoscopes News & Politics In the Magazine Weddings Newsletter Follow Other Editions Your Privacy Choices Privacy Notice Terms Of Use Skip to Content Newsletter Subscribe Search Sign in Sign in Subscribe Newsletter Subscribe Search Fashion Beauty Culture Shopping News & Politics Horoscopes In the Magazine Video My Bookmarks Newsletter US Sign In Your Privacy Choices Privacy Notice Terms Of Use Fashion Beauty Culture Shopping News & Politics Horoscopes In the Magazine Video More Culture Movies & TV The Liberation of Carrie Coon The Liberation of Carrie Coon The Gilded Age actress brings her astounding talent to a rare starring film role. By Sara Austin , Photographed by Norman Jean Roy. Styled by Alex White. Published: Nov 10, 2026 Save Article Share Article Norman Jean Roy Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy. 9 min read “We just need the women back in charge. This whole patriarchal structure is not working out,” Carrie Coon tells me cheerfully, two minutes after we’ve met. Our conversation follows from there, touching on Hollywood double standards, raising children in a traumatizing world, and our own mortality. “I just don’t have time for small talk,” says the Emmy-, Tony-, and Golden Globe-nominated actress. “Maybe that’s obvious.” Meaty is what Coon does. Raised in a large, working-class family in Ohio, she started out in Midwestern theater; she met her husband, the actor and playwright Tracy Letts, on a Chicago production of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (The couple now lives in suburban New York with their two school-age children and Letts’s infamous collection of 13,000-plus DVDs.) Coon made her feature film debut, improbably, as Margo Dunne in David Fincher’s Gone Girl —“I’d probably been on camera 15 days before I did that movie”—and then moved immediately to a career-defining role as grieving mother Nora Durst on HBO’s The Leftovers . Those performances began a run of sharp, grounded, and casually funny work in projects including The Post and His Three Daughters . The actress also single-handedly justifies a subscription to HBO Max, whether for her cathartic, eight-minute closing monologue in The Leftovers ; her viral monologue about middle-aged friendship on season 3 of The White Lotus ; or, lately, her role as indefatigable social climber Bertha Russell on The Gilded Age . Her new film, The Liberation , offers Coon a rare big-screen lead role as Rita Cooper, an assistant bank manager who upends her life after meeting the leader of a women’s commune (Lily James). Rita’s first attempts to let loose and dance within the group, awkward and touching, challenged Coon to unlearn her own physical ease (“I go crazy at a wedding,” she says). But by the film’s devastating end, Rita has wholly transformed. The project is director Guy Nattiv’s effort to understand the story of his grandmother, who survived the Holocaust as a child only to join a cult in the 1980s. “So often with cult documentaries, we stand outside of it because the gurus seem so ridiculous in hindsight,” Coon says. “Guy humanizes every decision Rita makes along the path. It doesn’t seem so foreign, and it’s much harder to hold yourself apart from her story.” Norman Jean Roy Dress, Alaïa. Earrings, bracelet, rings, Bulgari. Festival audiences have left the film shaken, she adds, although “people don’t immediately know why they’re so unsettled. A woman leaves her children, and it feels unnatural to us. But I think there’s something deeper going on that has to do with the fact that the social rules we’re living by are completely fabricated, and that we are living according to them by tacit agreement only. And this woman chose to walk away from all of that. Now, did she join a cult? Yes. But given her trauma, who are we to say what she needed to heal from that most unspeakable horror she experienced as a child?” Finding empathy for complicated people, Coon says, is the key to acting, and more. “Empathy is the whole game. And empathy is the thing we’re missing the most. There’s been a war on empathy because in the authoritarian endgame, that’s the only way to justify setting people against one another so that they’re not coming for the people at the top. Our antidote to that hopefully can be, should be, art.” Does she sometimes worry that she’s created a bit too much empathy for The Gilded Age ’s Bertha and her robber baron husband? The new season finds her character in a vulnerable and relatable place, unsteady in a marriage that had been her safe space. “We talk all the time about how we’re humanizing that class,” she says of her castmates. “But here’s the thing: If you knew any billionaires for real, [you’d see] they’re not naturally charismatic. So we’re not representative of the billionaire class in that way. We’re way too charming and sexy.” On a role that changed everything I remember arriving for Gone Girl in Cape Girardeau, Missouri. The cast was so excited for me and so welcoming. They were so moved by my story, that I had no business being in that movie, and there I was, and they all recognized how extraordinary that was for me. And so that process for me was a joyful one, in which I learned a lot because I also got along great with David [Fincher], and he taught me so much about being on camera. Oh my goodness, it was so scary. He could have fired me, but instead he taught me things. Norman Jean Roy Dress, Hermès. Earrings, rings, Bulgari. On the pressure to be “ageless” Of course, women should do what they want to do to feel their best, to not be depressed. However, it is worth questioning what we have internalized and where that choice is coming from. My experience, as I’ve watched this augmentation take over my industry—and then everything else, because my industry leads those conversations—I find it so alienating. When I see an actress who’s so far down the road that I do experience their face not moving, I don’t have as much empathy for them in their performance. I don’t have the mirror neurons. And my baseline is, “Oh, I see your fear. You’re afraid to die, and you’re afraid to get old.” And for me, every choice you make is coming out of that fear. I personally am not interested in living my life from that place. I’m not interested in making artistic choices from that place, because I would rather come to terms with the fact of my death, which will happen, because I don’t want to be unprepared. I guess that means I make a choice personally not to do anything to myself, and maybe that means my career has five more years in it. Oh, well, I’ll do something else. On the best part of Hollywood The best part is the people. That’s a myth about Hollywood that there’s some sort of rampant narcissism, but in fact, actors are some of the most curious people I’ve ever met. And the crews—they work these tremendous hours and everybody has to do their job well. I would hold it up as an example to any industry, because of what we accomplish—these are people from all walks of life, all socioeconomic classes, and we work together every single day and we make something, and I find it extraordinary every time we do it. On a woman in Hollywood she admires I love the way Christine Baranski moves through the world. She’s been in the business a long time. She raised her family while she was at the height of her powers, and I really value her input. She’s an old-school dame. She’s both political and classy. She always meets the moment, and I love having those conversations around the business with her. Norman Jean Roy Jacket, Hermès. Earrings, necklace, Bulgari. On friendships with other actresses I came to female friendship late. I was a tomboy and I had brothers, and I’m sure I wasn’t a great friend in my early years. And, oh my gosh, all I want is female friendship. I want to make those phone calls when I need advice. I want to go on long walks with women. And if my husband dies, he keeps joking, “Oh, your second husband’s going to love this couch.” I’m like, “No way I’m doing this again.” Not because I don’t love him, not because he’s not a great feminist, but because I’m ready for the crone years. I just want to get a bunch of women together. We’re going to cook. We’re going to talk about menopause. We’re going to have a book club. We’re going to dance naked in the moonlight because we don’t care. That’s what I want. And I didn’t know I needed it. On what still needs to change for women in Hollywood We know that it’s hard for women to get a first feature made. And even when their first feature is wildly successful, getting a second one made is nearly impossible. They don’t get offered the big tentpole movies. And if they screw one of those up, heaven forfend, they’ll never get a second chance to make anything. It’s such a punishing system. It’s not a meritocracy. Women never get a blank check. We have to justify every choice we make, and then we have to explain every mistake. The double standard is so unfair. It’s also really hard for new talent to break out. Capitalism is driving the industry, so therefore we are always going to make the safe choice. You’re going to see the same five men, the same five women starring in films every year. It’s not because they don’t deserve those opportunities—there’s a reason why these people are beloved actors—it’s just that then it’s very hard for anyone else to have a crack at things. Something like The Liberation is so exciting for me, because I don’t have access to leading roles in film. I have to fight for every [role]. Which is fine; I’m a fighter. But it reflects the reality of how little work there is to go around. On Hollywood mergers Corporate consolidation is bad for every consumer in any sector. I think it’s particularly corrosive for art, because it leads to gatekeeping and censorship. And it’s not just the news—when you have a few people controlling storytelling, that’s dangerous. So I’m worried about the identity of some of those brands. I mean, I’m an HBO gal. I’m very eager to see how HBO comes out of this: if they can have that same identity of making challenging, interesting, and edgy work, or if we’re going to get soft around the edges everywhere. I mean, I’m not interested in that. None of us are interested in that. So I hope they can maintain some identity inside of the merger, but no, it’s bad for everybody. It’s just basic economics. When three big companies are running the show, we’re going to pay more, and we’re going to get less. Norman Jean Roy Coat, Gabriela Hearst. On the theater-to-Hollywood pipeline I used to love speaking to students, and now when I speak to students, I feel I have very little to offer them. My story is not going to be their story. We have less funding for the arts than we’ve ever had in this country, and that means that every single cultural institution, museum, ballet, opera, theater—they’re all fighting for the same money right now, which is drivel. And that, of course, affects what theaters can program, because when they rely on ticket sales, they can’t take as many risks, and that means we’re not developing the next generation of young artists, playwrights, actors, anybody, and that’s impoverishment. The Kennedy Center is maybe going to be literally torn to the ground before anybody can stop it. And they were not in debt; the story about it is a lie, which we all know is a lie, and yet here we sit powerless in the face of this destruction. The only thing I can hope for is the innovation we’re seeing from young people in film, particularly. They’re making their own work with very little money, and they’re distributing it. We’re seeing these little projects break through and become massive hits, and we’re bringing young people back to the theater. So there’s always a chance that we can innovate, but boy, do we need government funding in addition to that. On keeping her children’s lives private Our children are being raised in a very different way than when we grew up. Tracy grew up in a small town in Oklahoma. I grew up in a small town outside of Akron in Ohio. My kids are being raised in an area of extraordinary privilege. We don’t know how to raise them in this environment, so we’re trying to pretend like it’s not like that. I also want to protect them from having to wrestle with [celebrity] so early, with whatever that does to a person’s ego. It’s so hard to be a kid. My kids are both pandemic kids, really. All these kids are struggling socially. And I don’t want to make it worse. I don’t need to trot my children out publicly. When my son is 16, and I make a project that he might enjoy—he loves a horror movie, for example—and he wants to come along [to the red carpet] and he’s old enough to make that decision for himself, great. I’d love to have him, because he’s a lot of fun. They’re probably going to be deeply disinterested, because they just want us to be home. Lead Image: Jacket, Hermès. Earrings, necklace, Bulgari.
